title: Is Claude Code really that much better than Codex for game development?
author: Illustrious_Exit_691
selftext:
Hey everyone,



I'm currently working on my first game in Unreal Engine 5. It's still pretty early in development, and I don't have much coding experience, so I've been relying a lot on AI.



I've mostly been using ChatGPT and Codex so far, but lately I keep seeing people on Reddit and X using Claude Code for pretty much everything. Some of the stuff people are building with it is honestly crazy, and it's making me wonder if I'm missing out.



Is Claude Code actually that much better than Codex, especially for game development? Or is it just more popular right now?



I'm also curious about the $20 Claude Pro plan. I usually spend several hours a day working on my game, so would the limits be a problem?



Just trying to figure out what makes the most sense before spending money on another subscription. Thanks!

comments.author: batmessiah
comments.body: The big thing I’ve noticed between my $20 subs between the 2 is that Claude is a far greater value and gives you a LOT more tokens.  I’ve upgraded to Claude Max and it gives TONS of compute.

replies.author: Illustrious_Exit_691
replies.body: Would the $20 Pro plan be enough for someone working 4–5 hours a day? I'm worried about hitting the limits too often.

replies.author: MidSerpent
replies.body: You’ll probably hit limits

replies.author: Patera-Milenko
replies.body:
You will hit limits for sure. If this is your budget, my best suggestion is to learn within that budget. 

Once you really "need" more compute look at it at that point. 

It might not be great advice if you want to move fast but that how I'm learning with the Ai as I go. 

Got it too setup lessons and let me try my hand at things etc. It's a lot more tokens to do that though but it's letting me learn and actually check code as I go. 

It's most likely a best use case for you vs your goal and any time lines you have but starting small doesn't hurt as much

replies.author: Minute-Animator-376
replies.body: 2xclaude 200 sub 1x100, codex 100$ (was on 200$ plan so practically nearly 500$ now), google on 30$, meshy 20$. I will use 100% of all in a week. Although I don't see a need for one 200$ sub now as it rather forced. I started with 100$ sub during prototype stage and it was more than enough. It looked like shit but core gameplay was fun and worked. For AAA feel and due to massive scope creep I was able to brute force a lot in 2 months and sleepless nights, I would compare the results to small studio working for years on a game. Now when core gameplay, mechanics, vfx are done and especially workflow and ways of working/best practices are battle tested etc are done finishing the game gets much cheaper and 1 200 sub will be cancelled, i would throw chat gpt into trash even with a free resets. It is not worth it vs claude. But I use it for image gen and other stuff outside of a game.

replies.author: Cygnusbeats
replies.body:
Opus can do the same for anything that you think astra is better at, is probably the instructions your giving the model thats limiting you at the time when doing voxels por example. 

By workflow I mean: Create a plugin where you have everything that you want that opus do when building games. What to use, example: Use blender headless for all the game assets, if you can’t reach a professional level of modeling using only blender use generative image generation and then create it in blender based on the image created. 

This is only an example but sky is the limit, it’s only that a 20usd sub won’t take you far when creating games.

I have my models building very detailed characters only using blender, then animating them, and if it doesn’t look profesional or well made, it will continue to criticize it until it looks good and then will show me the final result

replies.author: Salt-Freedom-2419
replies.body: Can you give me an exmaple? I'm using both. I tend to switch around when one isn't giving me results, but it is as often one as the other. E.g. Astra didn't really nail the water for my pirate game, so I made claude do it. Claude didn't impress me with voxel characters for my minecraf ripoff, so I let Astra handle it. My RTS needed low poly hard surfaciing modelling. So I built a tool. Astra botched the gui, so I gave the job to Claude. Claude however didn't really know how to use the tool, so I gave it to Astra... etc and so on.

comments.author: FuzzyBench3638
comments.body:
Codex for me is better for planning ideas. I can have astray and think about things, mockups imagegen for a blender pipeline. But codex always frustrate me when I'm building. Claude code I then review the finding and build in. It gets messy always trying to improve.

I feel like we are asking genies for wishes and they build is rube Goldberg solutions. It's our job to keep it tight. Use SDLC and try not to confuse the genie. All the things were trying to improve also break when openAI and anthropic update as there trying to fix the issues too. Good luck!

replies.author: Illustrious_Exit_691
replies.body: That makes a lot of sense. I've definitely had AI overcomplicate simple things before lol. How do you usually keep it on track? Do you plan everything out before letting it code?

replies.author: FuzzyBench3638
replies.body: I usually plan things out trying to find the gaps I know it will struggle on. Ask it “grill me, improvements?” with a frontier model. There are skills for that. I plan out long builds and then go to sleep and hope they work out lol. You have to be careful not to “guide it” to much they say “ok he said he didn't like it but it was perfect I MUST change things”

comments.author: Economy_Bedroom3902
comments.body: Claude code is very good at software related tasks.  It's biggest strengths are actually mostly in cheaply filtering signal from noise in indexing the codebase, and in debugging very big files, like log files.  Those don't necessarily make it objectively smarter, but they often make it less expensive to get similar results because they move some of the work that is hard for AI agents working on their own into the deterministic space where the work is being done for the agent before the agent gets started.

comments.author: RandomCSThrowaway01
comments.body:
Depends on what you are doing with it.

For full vibe coding slop extreme when you have no idea what you are doing and want one shotting - yes, right now Opus is better. Simply because it's a bit stronger model so it takes it longer before codebase starts rotting and it starts spinning in circles. You also have Sonnet which is essentially infinite on 100+ USD plans - whereas on Codex you get like 2h of Astra a week on equivalent plan (and Sol is a step down + it's pretty slow which you do notice if you decide to use it to, for instance, 3D model you something).

But if it's an assistant and you do read what it's producing, correct it when it goes over the top and you do work in Unreal itself properly and just ask it to expose you necessary fields etc - they are comparable. One big thing OpenAI has going for it is built in image generator whereas for Anthropic you pretty much have to connect it to NanoBanana or GPT Sunburst and pay about 6 cents per picture. Which arguably is useful for textures, concepts etc and it starts adding up.

Opus 5.5 is ultimately just a stronger model than Sol which means it navigates codebases better and is somewhat smarter at guessing what you want. Admittedly however in either case you still need to be specific in your requirements and occasionally explicitly even ask a competing model for a code review and a refactor (honestly Opus reviewing Sol or vice versa helps with code quality a fair lot so a $20 plan from the other brand tends to be worth it).

>I'm also curious about the $20 Claude Pro plan. I usually spend several hours a day working on my game, so would the limits be a problem?

Yes. $20 isn't a lot of usage. If by "several hours a day" you mean that LLM is working non-stop for more than 1 then you will be hitting limits.

comments.author: mrpoopistan
comments.body:
Here is my case for each, since I use the $20 account for each.

Claude Code

Opus 5.5 is better at relentless iteration. If you need it to work through lots of little crap, Opus will do a good enough job. It very much uses a "move fast and break things" approach that will be familiar to coders from certain environments. The tradeoff is that Opie ships lots of working code that isn't well-optimized. Opie does have more of an indpendent streak, for good and bad, mostly good.

Opie's biggest strength is that you can tell it"just make this work" and it will make it work. How efficient that work is is another question.

Codex

You get Astra, which is nice if you need to work out something absurd, like complex physics. Astra is also a good starting point for gather SOTA research and then feeding it to Opie or Sol.

Sol is perfectly capable of doing the same sort of work as Opie. The big difference is that Sol understands what the hell optimization is when you ask it. Generally, Sol thinks at long timelines and is more interested in getting things perfect on the first try, for good and bad.

My current workflow

I like to assemble and iterate everything quickly in Claude Opus, then take the mess over to Sol to clean up. Especially if you care about things like frame pacing, Sol is better at this.

comments.author: ButterflyMundane7187
comments.body:
They both have their pros and cons, and things change with every release. I use both Claude and Codex, as well as Google Antigravity. They all have their strengths and weaknesses.

For example, I've had problems getting Claude to help me disassemble old game code because of copyright restrictions, while Codex has worked great for reverse-engineering games from the 1980s. That's been my experience with older games, though I wouldn't assume the same applies to newer titles.

comments.author: DigitalLeprechaun
comments.body:
For starters, what's better today probably won't be tomorrow and then will be the day after. This space changes very quickly. Assuming top line models, for UE5 development Claude is, in my opinion, better. It creates better UMG and Blueprints for sure. C++ is on par. Claude often thinks too much though and I find it works best in a harness being guided by Codex.   
  
I know subs cost, but really, regardless to which you end up using, I'd strongly suggest subbing to both and pitting them against each other to review code/ideas/etc. Or better yet, Use one to orchestrate the other.

With any type of asset or layouts, you'll blow though a $20 plan pretty quickly. Lean on 3rd party services like Tripo3D, Higgs-field AI, FAL, ElevenLabs. These can help save you some time at a little extra cost. But Tripo3D can build a full fleshed out model from 4 GPTImage shots in about 10 minutes vs hours of Claude/Codex messing with Blender. Just let the agents fix any problems.
